claims.text: As-produced Q235 steel has a heterogeneous microstructure.
Pre-exposure thermal annealing homogenizes the microstructure of Q235 steel.
Annealing-induced microstructural homogeneity produces fewer defects in Q235 steel.
Annealing-induced microstructural homogeneity makes grain boundaries more uniform in Q235 steel.
Localized microstructural defects act as corrosion-initiation sites.
An annealed, homogenized microstructure promotes formation of a more continuous and adherent protective oxide film.
The protective oxide formed after annealing impedes electrolyte attack and reduces dissolution of corrosion-susceptible regions.
The annealing-associated oxide film is less susceptible to spallation and degradation under high-temperature thermal and chemical stress.
Annealed Q235 steel will undergo less corrosion-related degradation than untreated Q235 steel during aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C.
Annealed Q235 steel will exhibit lower mass change than untreated Q235 steel during high-temperature salt exposure.
Annealed Q235 steel will retain hardness better than untreated Q235 steel during high-temperature salt exposure.
Annealed Q235 steel will develop a more coherent oxide film with less spallation than untreated Q235 steel during high-temperature salt exposure.
At room temperature, untreated and annealed Q235 steel will both retain protective oxide films and show little difference in protection.
Unfavorable phase transformations induced by annealing could eliminate the corrosion-protection benefit.
The proposed annealing benefit may not occur in non-salt environments.
Annealing that is insufficient to homogenize the microstructure will provide a smaller corrosion-protection benefit.
The magnitude of corrosion improvement depends on annealing parameters and exposure duration.
